title: Fusion-aware shard allocator and collective scheduling playbook
content:
Summary:
This note captures an experimental design and runbook for a fusion-aware shard allocator combined with a collective-scheduling layer tailored for multi-GPU LLM serving. The goal is to reduce cross-GPU collectives, improve kernel throughput via opportunistic fusion, and maintain KV-cache coherence while preserving tight tail-latency SLOs.

Background and motivation:
We run into two recurring tradeoffs for production inference on GPU clusters: (1) latency-sensitive requests require minimizing cross-device collective overheads (NCCL all-reduce/all-gather) and (2) throughput-sensitive workloads benefit from kernel fusion and larger microbatches. Current shard allocators optimize for placement density or simple bandwidth heuristics but do not account for kernel-level fusion opportunities or KV-cache affinity. As a result we see suboptimal end-to-end cost and increased tail spikes during heterogeneous mixes.

Design goals (priority ordered):
- Keep P99 latency under configured SLO for interactive routes.
- Reduce total inter-GPU collective count per logical request by at least 25% on average.
- Preserve KV-cache hit rates during scaled resharding and autoscale events.
- Enable kernel fusion (attention + FFN where feasible) without increasing worst-case latency for short sequences.
- Provide a conservative fallback path when NCCL or interconnect is congested.

Constraints and assumptions:
- Fleet includes heterogeneous node types (A100, H100) with mixed NVSwitch/NVLink topologies.
- Models vary between causal and encoder-decoder; most heavy traffic is causal 70B/30B variants quantized to q4/q8.
- Customers may pin model versions; allocator must be able to respect reserved capacity (Dedicated) and private deployment policies.
- We can collect low-overhead telemetry (per-request stage timing, kernel durations, NCCL op counts).

Key ideas and mechanisms:
1) Fusion-aware shard allocator (FASA)
- Shard affinity groups: extend allocator to compute an affinity score between layers and candidate device groups. Score factors: kernel fusion potential (estimated if two adjacent layers run on same device, fusion avoids intermediate memory roundtrip), bandwidth locality (NVLink chain length), and KV-cache affinity (where cache pages are warm).
- Allocation objective: maximize sum(affinity_score) subject to device memory constraints and reserved capacity. This is a knapsack-like run with greedy heuristics for speed: seed placements for compute-heavy layers, then greedy expand to neighboring layers when fusion potential > threshold.
- Soft placement constraints: allow small cross-device splits for large layers but prefer intra-node fusion candidates.

2) Stage-level collective scheduling
- Instead of issuing NCCL ops immediately when a stage completes, introduce a short scheduling window (configurable 50-250us) to coalesce compatible collectives from multiple in-flight requests. This reduces collective count and increases NCCL efficiency without materially impacting latency for most requests.
- Compatibility rules: same collective type (all-gather/all-reduce), same participant set, compatible tensor dtypes/shapes.
- Adaptive windowing: shrink window when tail latency creeps up; expand when microbatching headroom exists.

3) Fusion-aware kernel prefetcher and executor
- At runtime, when two kernel launches (e.g., attention + rotary + linear projection) are predicted to be back-to-back and target same device, trigger a fused kernel code path (JITed fused operator) if sequence length and quantization profile match precompiled kernels.
- Maintain a small LRU table of fused kernels keyed by (op-pattern, dtype, seq_len_bucket). Fall back to unfused kernels when missing or if kernel would exceed memory transient.

4) KV-cache placement and migration policy
- Hot-shard sticky caching: when allocator places decoder layers across devices, bind KV-cache pages to the same affinity group. On resharding, migrate only the hot pages above an access frequency threshold and populate remaining pages via on-demand fetch to avoid high-bandwidth migrations.
- Consistency: on partial migration keep a device-local forwarder to replay requests requiring remote pages; use optimistic reads with validation tags to detect stale entries during fast failover.

5) NCCL fallback heuristics and hedging
- If a scheduled collective misses performance targets (detected via throughput/latency telemetry for the op), mark the group as degraded and optionally hedge: spawn a redundant smaller collective across a different device subset (e.g., split into two intra-node collectives) and merge results in software.
- This hedging is expensive; it should be applied conservatively for critical routes or when SLA is at risk.

Runtime architecture changes (high level):
- Allocation-time: FASA runs in the placement planner to create a per-model placement plan annotated with fusion groups and KV affinity. The planner emits placement_id and a compact placement descriptor consumed by the runtime.
- Execution-time: scheduler receives placement_id, applies collective coalescing windows, consults fused-kernel cache, and drives NCCL orchestrations. Telemetry emitted: per-request stage timings, collective counts, fused-kernel hits.

Metrics to track:
- P50/P95/P99 latency per route and model-version.
- Average collective ops per inference and per-token.
- Fused kernel hit rate and average fusion speedup multiplier.
- KV-cache miss rate and migration bandwidth during reshard events.
- Number of hedged collectives and their success rate.

Failure modes and mitigations:
- Fusion miss causing extra memory pressure -> detect via allocation failure; fall back to unfused path and record metric.
- Coalescing window increases tail -> adaptive shrink and bypass for latency-critical routes (marked in route config).
- KV migration storms on autoscale -> schedule migrations at low-traffic windows and enforce bandwidth caps.
- NCCL deadlocks if partial collective participants fail -> ensure timeouts and abort path that falls back to software merging.

Experiments and validation plan:
1) Simulation against recorded production traces: replay requests with candidate placements and compute estimated collective count and cross-node traffic.
2) Microbenchmarks: fused vs unfused kernel TL throughput for seq len buckets (16, 64, 256, 1024).
3) Canary rollout: small traffic slice (1%) on dedicated pool with telemetry gating. Metrics gate: no >5% increase in P99 and at least 10% reduction in collectives.
4) Stress scenarios: autoscale up/down with staged resharding and KV-migration bandwidth limited to ensure no traffic outage.

Operational runbook (short):
- Deploy placer + runtime changes behind feature flag.
- Enable for internal models first (non-customer).
- Monitor fusion-hit-rate, collective-count, p99. If p99 > SLO or fusion-hit drops sharply, disable fusion path.
- If hedging triggers frequently, investigate interconnect saturation or buggy topology mapping.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- Should certain route classes be marked fusion-ineligible by policy (e.g., function-calling routes with strict per-token latency)?
- How to integrate with Dedicated reserved-capacity sharding constraints more declaratively?
- Cost model: translate reduced NCCL ops to GPU-hour cost savings to prioritize heuristics.

Notes to implementers:
- Start with a user-configurable affinity threshold and a minimal fused-kernel table for the most common op patterns.
- Keep the collective coalescing window conservative by default (50us) and expose telemetry so SRE can tune.
- Reuse existing KV-cache instrumentation; add per-page access counters for migration hotness.

References and related artifacts:
- GH-PR-4821: initial placement proto and heuristics
- JIRA-SERV-927: KV migration throttling RFC
- Confluence: Multi-GPU Experiments (linked above)

Appendix: quick glossary
- Fusion group: contiguous layers placed on same device where launching a single fused kernel is possible.
- Collective coalescing window: short delay to aggregate collectives across in-flight requests for scheduling efficiency.
- Hedging: redundant execution of an op across alternate device groups to avoid tail due to a degraded collective.
